title: He Bet Everything on a Cricket Film Nobody Wanted — 25 Years Later, India Put It on a Stamp
excerpt: India Post honours Lagaan with a commemorative cover as Aamir Khan and Gracy Singh recreate their iconic scene — and the real headline? Aamir and Ashutosh Gowariker are going back to the crease together.
body:
Twenty-five years ago, Aamir Khan looked at a script about tax-paying villagers in colonial India challenging the British Raj to a cricket match, and decided it was worth betting his entire production house on. Nobody believed him. The poster had no heroine. The runtime was nearly four hours. The setting was a dusty village. And the sport? Cricket — a game most of the world couldn't follow.

Today, India Post unveiled a special commemorative cover for Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India, making it one of the few Bollywood films to receive the honour. Aamir Khan, now 61 and weeks away from his third wedding, stood alongside director Ashutosh Gowariker at the ceremony in Mumbai, looking very much like a man who knows he made the right bet a quarter century ago.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=JCBAP2wId5M

But the anniversary celebrations didn't stop at stamps.

!British Raj — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

*"Sachin's answer was characteristically casual: "We're playing Australia at Wankhede."**

Aamir Khan Productions released a video that sent the internet spiralling: Aamir and Gracy Singh — Bhuvan and Gauri, the couple that made an entire country believe that love and a googly could beat an empire — recreating one of their most iconic scenes from the original film. Twenty-five years later, same chemistry, same warmth, and a comment section full of grown adults admitting they cried.

It works because Lagaan was never just a film. For the Indian diaspora especially, it was the first time many NRIs saw their country's spirit projected on a global stage with genuine grandeur. The film became only the third Indian production ever nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film — a feat made more remarkable by the fact that it was produced independently by a 36-year-old actor who'd mortgaged his credibility to get it made.

A.R. Rahman's score remains one of his finest: Mitwa, Ghanan Ghanan, O Re Chhori — songs that still stop NRIs mid-scroll at family gatherings. The cricket sequences, choreographed with the precision of a Test match, needed authentic crowd roars. Enter Sachin Tendulkar, who recently revealed that Gowariker had approached him two years before the film's release, asking where to find the sound of a real Indian cricket crowd. Sachin's answer was characteristically casual: "We're playing Australia at Wankhede. Come record it." They did. Those are real Indian fans you're hearing in the film's climactic match.

The ensemble — Raghubir Yadav, Kulbhushan Kharbanda, Rachel Shelley, Paul Blackthorne — has aged into legend. Daya Shankar Pandey, who played the eccentric fast bowler Goli, recently revealed that the cast still has each other's numbers saved under their character names. Sourav Ganguly once asked him to demonstrate his bowling action live, convinced the film must have used CGI. It hadn't.

!Ashutosh Gowariker — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

The film returned to theatres for three days in mid-June, and Sony MAX has launched an entire film festival celebrating 25 years of Aamir Khan Productions, with Lagaan as the centrepiece.

But here's the real news buried in the anniversary glow.

Aamir Khan and Ashutosh Gowariker are reuniting. For a cricket film. Again.

The project is a period sports drama based on the life of Lala Amarnath, the first Indian cricketer to score a Test century — a story woven into the backdrop of the India-Pakistan partition. The script has been quietly developed with creative contributions from Rajkumar Hirani and writer Abhijat Joshi, which alone should make anyone who's ever loved Munna Bhai or 3 Idiots pay very close attention. Shooting is expected to begin in September 2026.

And Aamir isn't slowing down after that. The Lala Amarnath biopic is reportedly the first of three back-to-back films on his slate: next comes a startup-based comedy alongside Shraddha Kapoor, directed by Rahul Mody, followed by the long-rumoured sequel to 3 Idiots with Hirani directing. For a man about to get married on July 5, it's a staggering commitment — and a signal that Aamir Khan, at 61, is entering what might be his most ambitious phase yet.

For NRIs who grew up watching Lagaan on pirated DVDs in college dorms, or who saw it in packed theatres in Edison and Southall and Surrey, the anniversary means more than nostalgia. It's a reminder of what Indian cinema looks like when it swings for the boundary.

And with Aamir picking up the bat alongside Gowariker again, the next innings might be just as good.
